entities.summary:
Transnistria, officially the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic (PMR), emerged as a de facto independent state on September 2, 1990, though its effective sovereignty crystallized following the Transnistria War of March-July 1992. Located on a narrow strip of land between the Dniester River and the Ukrainian border, it remains internationally unrecognized by any UN member state, yet maintains its own government, currency, military, and customs system. Its existence fundamentally challenges international law regarding territorial integrity and self-determination, serving as a persistent "frozen conflict" hotspot in Eastern Europe that has shaped geopolitical discourse and regional stability since the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Key actors include the Moldovan government, the 14th Guards Army of the Soviet Union (later Russian), and local separatist leaders.

The genesis of Transnistria lies in the linguistic and political tensions of the late Soviet era. As Moldova moved towards independence and potential unification with Romania, the predominantly Russian-speaking and industrial eastern bank of the Dniester, fearing discrimination and loss of economic ties with Russia, declared its own sovereignty. This culminated in the 1992 conflict, where local militias, supported by elements of the Russian 14th Army commanded by General Alexander Lebed, fought against Moldovan forces. The war, which claimed hundreds of lives, ended with a ceasefire brokered by Russia, establishing a trilateral peacekeeping force (Russia, Moldova, Transnistria) and solidifying Transnistria's de facto independence, effectively creating a statelet that has functioned autonomously for over three decades.
